extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of photojournalism, journalism/media ethics instructors and interested general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and producing news photographs with attention to ethical standards: image integrity, editorial/contextual responsibility, and the line between enhancement and misrepresentation. Focuses on photojournalism in news media (image manipulation, captions, editors' role, credibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect human beings
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed by Julianne H. Newton as a core responsibility for photographers and editors; implies treating subjects with dignity, avoiding exploitative or dehumanising presentations, and considering harm when choosing or editing images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report clearly what you see
rubrics_metrics.description: To report clearly what they see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographers should aim to convey the observed situation accurately; clarity means not introducing elements or edits that obscure what actually occurred. The page contrasts clear reporting with composites that potentially alter perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be fair, accurate, and honest
rubrics_metrics.description: To be fair, accurate, and honest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core ethical standard for photojournalists and editors: avoid misrepresentation, present images and captions that reflect reality as faithfully as possible, and do not deceive audiences for dramatic effect or commercial gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use images fairly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images should be used in ways that do not mislead or manipulate viewers; fair use includes correct contextualisation, truthful captions, and not repurposing images to imply facts not supported by the visual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain integrity of content and context (NPPA guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing should maintain the integrity of the photographic images’ content and context. Do not manipulate images or add or alter sound in any way that can mislead viewers or misrepresent subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim NPPA Code of Ethics item cited on the page. Includes prohibition of manipulations that change meaning (composites, cloning, adding/removing people or elements) and altering audio in multimedia. The page uses Walski's composite and other examples to illustrate breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not manipulate images in ways that mislead or change message
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid edits (such as compositing) that change the message of a photograph or misrepresent the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central question posed about the Walski case is whether the composite altered the photograph’s message. Guidance: evaluate whether an edit changes the underlying informational content or meaning; if it does, it is unethical. Examples: Walski's composite versus original photos; cloning signs/people is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label photo illustrations and staged images
rubrics_metrics.description: Photo illustrations may be labeled as such and should be distinguished from documentary images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that photo illustrations are generally labeled, but also cautions many viewers won't notice labels. Best practice: clearly mark any image that is a composite, staged, or an illustration so audiences are not misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish permissible enhancement from deceptive alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Some editing (e.g., tonal/colour toning) can be acceptable; digitally cloning or adding/removing subjects is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page discusses examples (Patrick Schneider's colour adjustments versus cloning) and argues that tonal/colour adjustments that do not change content/message are often tolerated, while cloning or compositing that alters content is objectionable. Editors should set clear boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs should portray situations accurately regardless of artistic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Photojournalists must record and convey events truthfully and visually; accuracy takes precedence over artistic considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction between art photography and news photography: news photos primarily serve descriptive/documentary functions and should not prioritize aesthetics at the cost of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors and captioners share responsibility for image meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When a photograph is published it is contextualised by headline, caption and article; editors and writers can change or distort the photographic message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture editors, news editors and journalists influence the final meaning by selection and framing. The page warns that captions/articles can impair integrity intentionally or accidentally. Ethical practice requires careful, truthful contextualisation and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish original images and correct the record when alterations are discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: News organisations should be transparent when an alteration is found, e.g., publish original photographs and explain the ethical stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites newspapers publishing an editor's note with the originals after Walski's dismissal as an example of organisational response; transparency helps maintain or restore credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographers should provide originals to editors on request
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers should send only the original photographs (or make originals available) rather than a single edited composite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested procedural expectation from the page: sending originals enables verification and prevents disputes. In contentious cases, providing source files or originals allows editors to assess edits and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using images as propaganda or entertainment-first content
rubrics_metrics.description: News organisations should prioritise truthful reporting over sensationalism, profit motives, or propagandistic uses of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page criticises news-as-entertainment and profit-driven selection (blaring headlines, emotional imagery) and warns against using images to promote ideological agendas; ethical criterion: resist sensationalising or manipulating images for commercial/political ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about embedded journalism and proximity bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision of access through embedding with military or other actors can compromise objectivity and induce self-censorship or bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues embedded journalists may 'wear the uniform' and adopt values of those they cover, producing one-dimensional coverage. Ethical practice: maintain independence and seek multiple perspectives to avoid narrow framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations of photographic objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that photographs are chosen framings and products of perception rather than neutral windows on truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page uses Newton and Sontag to argue objectivity is a myth; ethical practice is to shift audience assumptions and avoid presenting images as 'complete truth'—use captions and context to clarify perspective and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scapegoating individuals for systemic editorial or organisational bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisations should not single out a photographer to conceal wider editorial bias or failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page suggests the LA Times may have used Walski as a scapegoat; ethical responses require addressing systemic issues (selection, framing, ownership bias) rather than only disciplining frontline staff to restore an appearance of integrity.
